newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade surplus soars, with more rises to come.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade surplus soars, with more rises to come.

text.p: Japan's contentious trade surplus rose dramatically in April, and though more rises are expected in the months ahead, the surplus should be kept in check by a stronger yen and a recovery in domestic demand, analysts said.

"Japan will suffer from drop in demand in the first half of this fiscal year (started April 1), which will be especially visible until June. Economic growth will be dependent on exports for the time being," said Hisashi Yamada, an economist at Japan Research Institute Ltd.
"But the pace of the growth will start shrinking from July. The growth in the surplus will be capped by the latter half of this fiscal year," he said.
Data released on Monday by the Ministry of Finance (MOF) showed Japan's overall customs-cleared trade surplus grew 163.7 percent to 831.48 billion yen ($7.23 billion) in April.

The sensitive surplus with the United States, which has already been grumbling about the growing trade imbalance between the two countries, soared 174.1 percent in April from a year earlier to 468.97 billion yen ($4.07 billion).
The figures were not adjusted for seasonal factors.
Economists attributed the jump mainly to car exports, which grew 32.1 percent in April from a year earlier, and slower growth in overall imports from sluggish domestic demand.

Japanese carmakers put priority on supplying their products to the domestic market in the January-March period to cope with strong demand ahead of the sales tax rise to five percent from three percent on April 1, they said.
But data for April-June will show carmakers shifting their focus abroad, amid strong growth in the U.S. economy and weakness in Japan, economists said.

A relatively weaker yen compared with a year ago has also fuelled a rise in exports, pushing Japan's trade surplus back up again after a long period of decline and threatening to inflame trade tensions.

"The United States may express concern over the rise in the surplus, but they won't take it up as a real serious issue. Unless the U.S. economy deteriorates suddenly, it won't become a big problem," Yamada said.
Satoru Ogasawara, an economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the rise in the trade surplus gave the Japanese government an incentive to keep the yen strong.
"Japan has been guiding the yen higher against the dollar to prove that it wasn't seeking economic recovery by using its exports," Ogasawara said.
Although the yen has strengthened to around 115 yen to the dollar compared with a 56-month high of 127.47 on May 1, Japanese exporters are still comfortable at this level, economists said.

The dollar briefly fell as low as 114.85 yen on the trade figures on Monday but the data was largely within expectations and the greenback soon bounced back to trade at around 115.60 yen, the same level as in late U.S. trading on Friday.

As the U.S. economy loses momentum later in the year and the Japanese economy continues to gain steam, "this suggests that the rise in the trade surplus will be capped and we won't see the sharp gains that many people are anticipating," said Andrew Shipley, an economist at Schroders Japan. ($1=115 yen)
